newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sacks top brass, prepares for Belarus deal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sacks top brass, prepares for Belarus deal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, in a vigorous display of authority over the armed forces, sacked Russia's two top defence officials on Thursday, accusing them of neglecting much-needed military reform.
He singled out Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and general staff head Viktor Samsonov for a televised tongue-lashing at a meeting of the Defence Council of military leaders.

"I am not simply dissatisfied, I am indignant over the state of reforms in the army and the general state of the armed forces," Yeltsin said angrily before he sacked them. "The soldier is losing weight while the general is getting fatter."
Yeltsin, who was backing reformist defence aide Yuri Baturin with his decision to sack Rodionov, then brought in the chief of the strategic nuclear forces Igor Sergeyev as acting minister.
He did not say exactly how Sergeyev should reform the armed forces but made clear that this time the military should fit into its austere budget.
"The armed forces should feel that they are in a reforming country with limited financial resources," he said.
Signalling firm support for his new reformist team in a tussle over the future of the military, Yeltsin appointed two liberal ministers to the powerful Security Council of senior officials.

The liberals, first deputy prime ministers Boris Nemtsov and Anatoly Chubais, will defend government policy in the opposition-dominated State Duma lower house on Friday, when deputies debate a government request to cut spending.

Ministers, worried by dismal tax revenues but determined to resist pressure to print money to pay overdue wages and pensions, are asking for spending cuts totalling 108 trillion roubles ($17.5 billion).
But the government made clear that the cuts would take place no matter whether the Duma backed them or not.
"Judging by debates in the chamber the deputies are likely to let the cabinet make the cuts and later approve them in parliament," First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin told RIA news agency.

"If the deputes say a resolute 'no' to the bill we are ready to cut spending without parliamentary approval. But then they should make appropriate changes to the budget legislation. We are ready for either option."

Russia's military reform and security policy depends heavily on the nature of its ties with the NATO alliance. Yeltsin is due to sign a document in Paris next week setting out its new relationship with NATO.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky hailed the deal as a diplomatic triumph, but he warned the alliance that offering membership to former Soviet republics would be like playing Russian roulette.

"We hope that sensible leaders in the West will not want to play Russian roulette," he said, referring to the daredevil game in which gamblers put one bullet in a revolver, spin the chamber, put the gun to their heads and fire.
Yeltsin, who wants to strengthen ties with neighbouring states before the NATO expansion, is due to sign a union charter with Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko on Friday.

The Kremlin said the two leaders, who have committed themselves to closer integration, met in Moscow and finalised the charter meant to fill in the largely declarative Union Treaty signed on April 2. It gave no details.
Interfax news agency quoted Lukashenko as saying that a disputed clause about the ultimate aim of the union had been withdrawn.

Yeltsin has spoken of Russia and Belarus merging into a single federative state by the end of the integration process but Lukashenko, unwilling to lose his own presidential status, said Belarus would remain a sovereign state.
Yeltsin is due to visit Ukraine next week, although Kiev's top security official said he had a "bad feeling" about whether the much-postponed visit would go ahead.
"A very active campaign has begun in Russian circles...aimed at breaking off President Boris Yeltsin's visit," Security Council secretary Volodymyr Horbulin said.

"Before (Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma's) visit to the United States there was a warm hope that everything would be fine...Now I have a bad feeling. But we'll our do our utmost to make this visit happen, without losing our dignity."

In a further display of authority Yeltsin refused to sign a controversial law claiming Russian ownership of art seized from Nazi Germany during World War Two. He sent it back to parliament, saying procedures used to adopt the law had violated the constitution.
